subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning a 1930s-style typewriter model with a root joint, sketching out approximate dimensions for width, depth, and height, and starting with a base plate sized to anchor the rest of the parts.

I'm working out the body shape by extruding a sloped side profile along the x-axis -- defining the outline points so the front is lower, the keyboard bank rises toward the back, and the body steps up into a taller rear block, while also planning the platen as a cylinder mounted above for the carriage.

For the paper, I'm sketching a thin sheet geometry that wraps from behind the platen, curves over its top, and angles forward in front near the type basket, approximating the path with a swept box section rather than a true lathe.

For the typed text, I'm designing a noise-based paint function so dark dashes appear only within the upright portion of the paper, using periodic line bands combined with horizontal noise to fake typewritten characters.

Now I'm setting up the keyboard geometry, planning four staggered rows positioned along a sloped surface.

Actually, rather than per-letter texture atlases, I'll make the key caps dark and overlay a small cream letter plane using an SVG texture with transparent background, so the letter appears to float above the dark disc — 40 small textures should be cheap enough.

Now I'm working out the keyboard rows (numbers, QWERTY, ASDF, ZXCV) and positioning each row along the keyboard's sloped surface using a normalized tangent vector, stepping row-by-row from front to back with consistent spacing.

Working out the keyboard layout geometry...

Now I'm thinking through the typebar basket design: the bars need to fan out in a semicircular arc with pivot points positioned around the printing point, each rod angled to converge toward the center when at rest.

I need to adjust the pivot ring radius to avoid colliding with the keys, pulling it in to 0.08 and shifting the center so bars sit cleanly on the body ledge. Each bar runs from its pivot up to a tip near the center point, built as a thin chrome rod with a tiny type-slug block at the end, spanning roughly ±85° across 29 bars, plus a base ring to anchor them.

I'm also adding a chrome rim sweeping around the pivot circle as an arc, computing the start point and sweep angle using right-hand rotation about the Y-axis to get the 170° arc right.

Now I'm sketching the back body outline behind the basket, defining coordinate points for the housing profile up through the pivot ledge at y≈0.115-0.12, adjusting the z-ranges so the ledge and pivot align with the ring radius.

For the side frame uprights, I'm planning two green support posts at x=±0.17 flanking the carriage, using a boxed profile with a sloped top extruded along the z-y plane to match the body's shape.

Now I'm sketching the platen as a black cylinder running along the x-axis behind the carriage, with small knobs capping each end outside the uprights.

Now I'm plotting the paper's curved path as it feeds up behind the platen, wraps over the top with a slight radius offset, and curls around the front edge before descending—using a sequence of curve points to get that natural paper-roll bend.

Working out the paper's curve coordinates...

Still working out the paper curl coordinates...

I'm figuring out how to render typed text lines on the paper, restricting them to the lower half and varying line lengths with a noise function so the right margin looks uneven and natural.

For the paper color I'm going with a warm cream tone and a dark ink shade, keeping the paint function scoped to the paper surface only. Now I'm working out the geometry for the chrome carriage return lever, positioning it at the left end of the carriage and curving it outward and upward with a bezier path.

Still shaping the lever path and knob...

I'm also laying out a small brass badge on the front face, extruding an oval outline with the right axis orientation so the thickness faces outward correctly.

For lettering, I'll add a separate decal plane positioned just in front of the badge surface, placed carefully at a z-depth that doesn't conflict with the body's front bevel faces.

Now I'm thinking through trim details: skipping feet and pinstripes for simplicity, but adding a chrome strip along the keyboard slope's bottom edge and top front edge, plus two ribbon spool discs near the top front corners of the basket area with small chrome cups.

I'm placing ribbon spool cylinders on the back block with black rings, considering a margin scale bar and a green paper table plate in front of the platen while skipping the paper support, and settling on specific hex colors for green, chrome, and brass tones.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy: a root joint at the base, plus a carriage joint with hinge-like role for the platen, knobs, paper, rails, bail, and lever, and a child lever joint under the carriage, keeping the structure simple rather than giving every key its own joint.

I'm computing key placement by mapping each row to a curved surface position using a tilt angle and normal vector, then spacing columns along that normal with row-specific stagger offsets for the typing rows.

Still working out key cap geometry...

For the letters, I'll generate small SVG textures per character, cached by character, rendering cream-colored bold serif text on a transparent background, then tally up the unique material colors needed across the keyboard: green, dark green, chrome, black, brass, and paper tones.

Now I'm figuring out part counts, with 117 keys and 58 bars, and working out the geometry for each type bar. I'm placing pivots along an arc and computing tip positions that rise toward the platen, adding small chrome slugs at the tips and thin chrome rods for the bars, keeping them straight rather than curved for simplicity.

I'm also computing a semicircular pivot ring using a y-axis rotation formula to sweep the rim shape around the typewriter's mechanism, with a tube radius of 0.004.

Now I'm checking that the basket's back wall, uprights, and typebar region don't collide given their z and x extents, then positioning the carriage rail as a thin bar resting above the basket.

Working through the uprights relative to the platen: they sit outside the platen's span, with a chrome axle rod running through them and black knobs with chrome hubs capping the ends, plus small chrome rings on the platen's own ends.

Now I'm placing the carriage lever near the knob — a short angled path from the knob area outward with a black ball tip, mounted on a lever joint — and positioning a paper bail rod across the front of the platen at a slight offset angle.

Checking the paper wrap path: it starts at the front wrap point, curves under the platen, and continues up the back, with the bail rod sitting just outside the paper radius so it clears it correctly. I'm also marking the typed text region on the back lower section of the paper, leaving the top area blank.

For the paper geometry itself, I'm building a thin box-section sweep along the carriage path with flat caps, keeping its top edge comfortably above the platen. I still need to settle on imports—likely sticking with createBuilder, catmull, arc, bezier, paint, and skipping noise in favor of simple sine-based variation for the typed lines.

Working out how the typed text breaks into words and letters using sine-based thresholds for speckling, then extruding the body with bevels and sharp corners, positioning the carriage parts symmetrically, and making sure the floor sits correctly under the paper stack.

Now I'm adding a chrome trim strip, brass badge, and ribbon spool cylinders at the back of the block, plus small rubber feet at the corners sized so they sink only slightly into the base. I'm also starting to set up the joint hierarchy for the mechanism, defining the base, carriage, and lever joints with their positions and hinge directions...

Writing part placement code...

Writing paper paint function...

Still refining paint bounds...

For texel density, I'm estimating the painted paper area is small relative to the total model, so the computed texel resolution comes out around 3700, capped at 4000 for sharp detail. Satisfied this covers only the paper region correctly, I'm ready to finalize and write out the full code.
